<reason>CON built one structural argument — a legally captive buyer cannot extract real price discipline — and sustained it through every round while forcing PRO into visible retreats: the outcomes contract shrank from avoided complications to in-year weight/glucose, and PRO conceded that a prescriber exception unlocks the non-preferred brand. CON answered both pressure questions with a direct "Yes" and turned them into weighing, whereas PRO's A1 (refunds for non-responders) was immediately absorbed by CON's "sellers price responders to cover refunds," and PRO's reply that this "kills every pharmacy contract" was met with the decisive distinction that other contracts sit on buyers who can drop the drug. PRO's strongest line — the plan still pays the complication bill — was blunted by CON's discontinuation/weight-regain point, the North Carolina spending example, and the observation that diabetics are already covered so the marginal mandated patient is pre-complication. CON's two clipped turns are a real execution cost and keep this from being dominant, but the content that survived carried the debate.</reason>
<best_rebuttal>CON's closing turn on PRO's signature line: "walking away from the pill is not walking away from the bill" — granted, but the mandate doesn't walk away from the bill either; with discontinuation and weight regain it "staples a second, larger, certain invoice in front of it." This neutralized PRO's only remaining live route to victory.</best_rebuttal>
